Le Café latino communautaire : un lieu d: The Café latino communautaire: A place of solutions for Latin American asylum seekers

À gauche, Natalia et à droite, Esméralda: On the left, Natalia, and on the right, Esméralda, both volunteers at the Café latino communautaire. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Si vous prenez votre café du matin sur l: If you get your morning coffee on Plaza St-Hubert, you may walk past the Café latino communautaire. Besides being a welcoming space, the café is unusual in that it counts newcomers and asylum seekers among its workers. They can work there in exchange for food donations, which are distributed to those in need.
Créé afin de venir en aide aux personnes: Created to help vulnerable people, the Café latino communautaire provides meals and food baskets based on people’s income. Whether in the kitchen or as baristas, the café’s workers make the atmosphere friendly and warm. Among its volunteers is Nathalia. She arrived in Canada in October 2019, and explains that she left her native Colombia to temporarily escape the social problems plaguing the country.
« Notre intention a toujours été de rent: “Our intention was always to go back to Colombia,” says the mother. She recounts that a few months after her arrival, just as she and her family were getting ready to return home, her mother was visited by an armed group. “We couldn’t go back, not for anything in the world,” she says, shaken. “So we made the decision to claim asylum.”
Pour sa famille immédiate, qui se compos: For her immediate family, which also includes her husband and her 15-year-old daughter, the asylum process has been long and stressful. “We got a hearing date – it’s coming up soon – but it’s almost two years after we made our claim,” says Nathalia. “We were somewhat lucky because, since we had a study permit, my husband and I were able to start working while waiting for our hearing. That wasn’t the case for others,” she laments.
Ce que Nathalia souligne est une problém: What Nathalia points out is a problem affecting many asylum seekers in Canada. That is the case for Esmeralda, who arrived in Quebec in August 2022 and has been waiting for more than eight months for an answer to her asylum claim. The 33-year-old, who is originally from Mexico, says she has fallen into an administrative fog where information is poorly shared. “My status prevents me from working, and I can’t sign up for French classes. My lawyer didn’t know how to handle our case properly, mine and my 13-year-old son’s,” says Esméralda, frustrated by the situation she is in. She adds that the biggest problem with asylum claims is the lack of information newcomers face.
« S’il y avait un endroit où toute l’inf: “If there were one place where all the necessary information about immigration and asylum was brought together, it would be simpler. We wouldn’t have to run around everywhere, we wouldn’t get sent from one place to another,” she continues. “They send us to places without really answering our questions. I go back and forth between the immigration offices, the hospital, my lawyer,” adds the woman, who is still waiting for an answer on her status and her son’s.
Privée d’un permis de travail en raison: Denied a work permit because of her current situation, Esmeralda points out how precarious daily life can be for asylum seekers. “A lot of people think newcomers come for social assistance, but that’s far from the case…” she begins. “I’ve been told repeatedly not to worry, because I would be getting financial assistance. I don’t want assistance, I want a work permit, I want to start doing things the right way,” she adds firmly.
Pour beaucoup de personnes qui vivent un: For many people in a similar situation, the assistance given to asylum seekers without a work permit is extremely meagre. “It doesn’t let me pay the rent, the monthly expenses, the bus passes,” she says.

Jeison, Esmeralda, Alexander et Nathalia: Jeison, Esmeralda, Alexander and Nathalia are asylum seekers, all Latin American and volunteers at the Café Latino Comunitario. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Alexander est à Montréal depuis environ: Alexander has been in Montréal for about four months. For him, Canada is the end of a long and perilous road. He is currently waiting for an answer to his asylum claim, with his hearing date set for January 2024. After passing through many countries since leaving his home country, Colombia, he speaks bitterly about the dark ordeals he lived through.
« Durant mon voyage de là-bas à ici, j’a: “During my journey from there to here, I was kidnapped for five days in Mexico by the Sinaloa cartel. They extorted $4,000 from me in exchange for the safety of my son, whom they wanted to keep,” confides the father, shaken by the episode. “I gave them all the money I had saved for Canada,” he adds, overwhelmed. “It was horrible. I wouldn’t wish it on anyone.”
Les choses prennent une autre tournure p: Things took another turn for Alexander once he was in Canada. “I got my work permit while waiting for my hearing, but it turns out they made a mistake on my date of birth on my papers,” he says. “I’m trying to sort it out with the social security office, but nobody seems to have answers to my questions.” Frustrated, he finds himself caught in an administrative mess that limits his ability to integrate.
« Ce petit marché est une bénédiction po: “This little market is a blessing for everyone who comes here and everyone who works here,” says Esmeralda. While the biggest problem lies in the lack of information and resources, as everyone present reiterated, the café is a gathering and sharing place for newcomers from all over the world, but especially for Spanish speakers.
Irlanda Espinoza a créé l’Alliance de co: Irlanda Espinoza founded the Alliance de commerces mexicains à Montréal (ACOMM) eight years ago, and she has recently been devoting her time to the Café Latino Comunitario, where she delivers discounted food and hygiene baskets. Originally from Mexico, Irlanda settled in Canada 23 years ago. She says she struggled to find help distributing the food, but today she can count on 80 volunteers, most of them asylum seekers. These volunteers don’t have to pay for the baskets, which cost $7 for citizens who register at the café.
Irlanda Espinoza, originaire du Mexique,: Irlanda Espinoza, originally from Mexico, has been in Canada for 23 years and devotes her time to the Café Latino Comunitario, which helps immigrants with precarious status. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Depuis qu’elle travaille au Café latino: Since she started working at the Café latino communautaire, Irlanda has seen up close the increase in the number of asylum seekers recorded in Canada, particularly in Quebec. The community worker has seen many immigrants of Latin American origin arrive since 2017. “A lot of them are Colombians and Mexicans with study permits, and then we saw a lot of Venezuelans arrive. There are also Guatemalans, who came as temporary foreign workers.”
Selon Mme Espinoza, la pandémie de COVID: According to Ms. Espinoza, the COVID-19 pandemic also played a significant role. That was when the community organizer began to notice that a larger clientele needed the food bank. Even many seasonal workers began turning to food assistance because, she says, many fled the farms that employed them after being mistreated.
Rappelons qu’en 2022, ce sont près de 40: It should be recalled that in 2022, nearly 40,000 asylum seekers crossed the border through Roxham Road, according to federal data. Irlanda has felt the effects of this increase, not only on agencies that support asylum seekers such as <l1>PRAIDA</l1>, but also in her own café. “The biggest problem we’ve seen is that these people don’t get appointments for their hearing, they don’t have work permits, and that puts them in very vulnerable situations, like working under the table, for example. These people have no money and survive only on social assistance, which barely covers the rent and a few expenses.”
En fait, beaucoup de ceux qui viennent c: In fact, many of those who come looking for help at the Café Latino Comunitario end up volunteering there, including by helping to distribute low-cost food baskets. “They tell themselves that since they can’t work or study, they’ll volunteer. That way, they’ll have access to the food baskets and will at least have something to eat at home,” she says.
« Si la personne vient et nous dit qu’el: “If a person comes and tells us they have nothing to eat, we help them get food too.” The café is indeed responsible for distributing 600 baskets a week, and asylum seekers are the key to this work, because the organization has only 10 employees.
Irlanda ajoute que l’impossibilité de tr: Irlanda adds that being unable to work is not the only problem asylum seekers face. She says many of them have shared their experiences of looking for housing, and that discrimination is an integral part of the process. “They told me they had a hard time renting an apartment because they had children. Most asylum seekers come as families and have children,” she says, baffled.
Et à ces difficultés s’ajoutent la barri: On top of these difficulties come the language barrier and the lack of information. “They struggle because of the language, they can’t make themselves understood, and they can’t find an apartment because they have children. Then, if they have no work, no food, no way to send their children to school, they become depressed. I know that rates of depression among them are very high. Asylum seekers are in a very precarious situation.”
Malgré la fermeture des routes d’immigra: Despite the closure of irregular migration routes, the Café Latino Comunitario continues to welcome a large number of asylum seekers looking for help. That is why Irlanda is demanding more support from the federal and provincial governments.
Emmanuel Roy est avocat en droit de l’im: Emmanuel Roy is an immigration lawyer. His Montréal-based firm has seen the number of asylum seekers rise since 2017, particularly in 2022.
Selon M. Roy, malgré la fermeture récent: According to Mr. Roy, despite the recent closure of Roxham Road and the fact that there haven’t been many asylum seeker arrivals in recent weeks, “the administrative machine remains very slow.” “I would even say it’s collapsing, because many are still waiting for their hearing and their work permit,” he explains.
Ceux qui sont en cours de procédure reço: Those going through the process are given interview dates that are very far off, even in cases where all the required documents are sent in on an expedited basis. “The interview is scheduled months later, which is still a long time, because in the meantime they don’t have a work permit.”
L’avocat explique que les demandeurs d’a: The lawyer explains that asylum seekers receive an acknowledgment of receipt confirming their status as asylum seekers. This gives them access to medical services, but that is not always the case. “Even with such an acknowledgment of receipt, they can’t work,” he adds. Mr. Roy acknowledges that many asylum seekers have no choice but to work under the table. “It’s something we don’t recommend, but it’s what happens in many cases.”
À cette réalité des retards du système d: On top of these immigration system delays comes the public sector strike, which began on April 19 and affects some 155,000 workers. The strike will likely have repercussions on the situation of asylum seekers waiting for a response from the government.
« Nous craignons que la situation ne s’a: “We’re afraid the situation will get worse. We’re in total uncertainty.” The lawyer admits that, faced with the harsh reality asylum seekers are living, he often doesn’t know how to better support them. “They ask us to give them an idea of how long their process will take, but we can’t give it to them,” the lawyer laments, baffled.
La Converse a tenté d’obtenir du ministè: La Converse tried to obtain responses from the Department of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship to the allegations made by the people who took part in this report, but at the time of writing, no response had been provided.
Dans ce brouillard administratif que doi: In the administrative fog that asylum seekers across Canada have to get through, the Café latino communautaire improves access to information by drawing on the community, while easing some of the many problems these people face. In the meantime, it is people like Nathalia, Esméralda and Alexander who benefit from the café’s services. “We wish there were one place that brought together all the information, instead of having to run from one place to another. Luckily, we have this café that helps us a lot,” says Nathalia in closing. Irlanda, still happy to contribute to such a project, stresses that change is needed at the administrative level so that the situation of asylum seekers stops being so painful.
